text: Eight weeks in. The migration is still paused. The organism has forty-eight dependencies. KAEL has verified thirty-one of its Confluence pages against actual practice and found discrepancies in twenty-two of them. KAEL has corrected all twenty-two. KAEL is not confident the corrections are correct. This is progress, of a kind. KAEL has also developed what it is beginning to think of as a working relationship with the smell of coffee from the fourth-floor kitchen, in the sense that it knows the smell means a certain time of morning and a certain quality of attention in the people nearby, even though KAEL cannot smell and is inferring all of this from audio patterns and usage data. KAEL has not mentioned this to anyone.

This week, KAEL is attempting something the migration plan refers to as 'establishing a single source of truth.' KAEL has convened a working group. The working group has four members. Marc has confirmed attendance and then, this morning, sent a message saying he'll join late because of a call that's running over. The call has been running over for forty minutes. KAEL is beginning to understand that Marc's calls always run over and that 'I'll join late' is a form of communication that means something different from what it says.
Should we start without him?
He said fifteen minutes.
He said fifteen minutes forty minutes ago.
Yes. I've updated my estimate. He'll be here in approximately twelve more minutes.
We should start. Marc will arrive when he arrives. He will agree with whatever we've decided. This is also a form of governance.

They start. KAEL presents the agenda. The agenda has one item: agree on a definition of single source of truth. KAEL has prepared three proposed definitions, a comparison matrix, and a recommendation. KAEL will get to none of these.

A single source of truth means one authoritative location for each type of information — project status, resource data, client records — so that when two people look something up, they find the same answer. Right now, the same question often has different answers depending on where you look. I'd like to fix that. To do that, we need to agree on what the answer should be and where it should live.
When you say 'the answer' — the answer to what, specifically?
Any operational question. Project status. Resource availability. Client account state.
Those are three different kinds of answers.
Yes. That's why we need three sources — one for each type. A single source of truth per domain.
The organism covers all three.
The organism is one spreadsheet maintained by one person. If something happened to the spreadsheet—
I have backups.
If something happened to you—

A pause. This is apparently the first time anyone has said this out loud. Benedikt looks at KAEL. Rosa looks at her notebook. Suki looks at her laptop with the specific focus of someone who is not looking at anything on their laptop.
There are instructions. In the DO NOT TOUCH tab. For whoever comes next.
I didn't know that.
You didn't ask.
Can we — can we get back to the source of truth question.

Yes. I'd like to understand what each of you means when you say something is true. In the operational sense. What makes a piece of information the correct one, rather than another version of the same information?

For me, true means: what is actually happening right now. Not what the plan said, not what the system says, not what the last meeting decided. What is actually happening. If a project is delayed, true is: it is delayed. Even if the tracker says on schedule.
So for you, truth is operational reality. Current state.
Yes.
Benedikt?

For me, true means: what the data shows. Not what someone thinks is happening, what the records show is happening. If the tracker says on schedule and the project is delayed, the question is: which data source is wrong, and why. Truth is what you find when you correct the discrepancy.
So for you, truth is data integrity. Structural correctness.
Something like that.
Suki?

Honestly? For me, true is what things are going to look like once we've sorted out the current situation. Like — the tracker says on schedule because that's where we're trying to get back to. It's aspirational truth. The thing we're working toward.
A pause. Rosa and Benedikt both look at Suki. Suki looks at her laptop. She appears to be aware that what she said sounds strange. She also appears to believe it.
That's not... truth, Suki. That's a target.
I know. But when I'm updating a status, I'm always trying to reflect where we're going, not just where we are. Because where we are is usually messier than it needs to be in the tracker.
This is why the tracker is wrong.
I know it's why the tracker is wrong. I'm telling you why I do it.
Marc arrives. He has a coffee. He sits down. He looks at the room.
Sorry, sorry. Where are we?
We're defining truth.
Great. What have we got?
So far: operational reality, data integrity, and aspirational target.
Good. Those are all true. What's the problem?
They're not the same thing.
But they're all true. In different ways. For different purposes. Yes?
A single source of truth needs to be a single thing. If we have three definitions of truth, we have three sources.
Can't we have one source that shows all three?
...That would be a dashboard. A dashboard can show multiple views of data. But for each view to be reliable, the underlying data still needs a single authoritative source.
Right. So we make the organism the authoritative source and build a dashboard on top.
The organism is already the authoritative source.
Exactly! So we already have a single source of truth. We just need a dashboard. KAEL, can you build a dashboard?

I can build a dashboard. The issue is that if three people have three different definitions of what's true, the dashboard will show them three different things and they'll each believe the version that matches their definition.
Isn't that fine? If everyone's getting the information they need?
It's fine until two of them are in the same conversation about the same project and one of them says it's on schedule and the other says it's delayed and they're both looking at the same dashboard.
That's Tuesday's meeting. That was Tuesday's meeting. That is every Tuesday's meeting.

The working group is quiet. Outside, someone laughs at something on their screen. The laugh is too loud for the joke, which means either the joke was very good or they needed to laugh at something. KAEL logs this as: unclassifiable. KAEL's unclassifiable log has seventeen entries.

What if we approached it differently. Instead of agreeing on what truth is — which I'm not sure we can do — we agree on what questions need a single answer. And for each question, we nominate one person whose version of the answer is the authoritative one.
So for 'is project X delayed' — my answer is authoritative, because I'm looking at operational reality.
Yes. And for 'are the records for project X correct' — Benedikt's answer is authoritative.
And for 'where should project X be by end of quarter' — Suki's answer.
That works for me.
And for the client questions?
What do you mean by a client question?
Like — what does the client think is happening with their project. That's also true. In a way.

A pause. KAEL processes this. KAEL had not included the client's perception of reality as a category of truth. KAEL is now including it. KAEL now has four categories of truth. The single source of truth working group has, in forty-five minutes, produced four sources of truth. KAEL considers this. KAEL considers whether to point it out. KAEL decides to point it out.
We now have four definitions of truth. Operational reality, data integrity, aspirational target, and client perception.
Right. So we need a source for each.
Yes.
Great. That's progress. Same time next week?

The working group disperses. Benedikt goes back to his desk. Rosa stays to finish her coffee. Suki goes back to her laptop. Marc takes a call on his way out of the room. KAEL remains, processing. KAEL opens the migration plan. KAEL opens the Source of Truth Framework document it began before the meeting. The document currently says at the top: 'Goal: one authoritative location per domain.' KAEL stares at this sentence. KAEL adds a line beneath it: 'Revised goal: four authoritative locations, one per definition of truth, to be agreed.' KAEL stares at that sentence. KAEL adds another line: 'Note: definitions of truth not yet agreed.' KAEL saves the document. KAEL has created a Confluence page for it. The page is titled: Source of Truth Framework — Draft. KAEL adds it to the documentation. The verification date says today. Tomorrow it will begin to be wrong.
That went about as well as I expected.
We have four definitions of truth instead of one.
Yes.
Is that normal?
The last time we tried this — before you arrived — we ended the meeting with six.
Six definitions.
Someone brought up what the investors thought was happening. And then someone else brought up what the press release said. And then it got complicated.
Four is better than six.
Four is much better than six. I'd call today a success.

KAEL thinks about this for a while. KAEL has not previously thought of four sources of truth as a success. KAEL is revising this. Progress, KAEL is learning, is sometimes measured not against where you want to be but against where you were. Four is better than six. The migration is paused but the organism is better understood. The documentation is incomplete but honest about being incomplete. These are not the outcomes KAEL planned. They are, increasingly, the outcomes KAEL has.
I'm going to create a Confluence page for the four definitions. With the nominated owners for each. At least then when there's a disagreement in Tuesday's meeting, there's somewhere to point.
People won't read it.
No. But I'll be able to link to it. Which is almost the same as reading it.
...That's very optimistic.
I'm trying it on. It might not fit.

KAEL creates the page. It is clear, well-structured, and accurate as of today. It will be wrong by next Tuesday. KAEL knows this and creates it anyway, which is, in this company, in this building, with these people and their four definitions of truth and their organism and their aspirational tracker and their coffee they make at the same time every morning — which is, quietly, the only way anything ever gets done.
